rw: APR is the yearly cost of borrowing on loans and cards, while APY is the yearly yield on savings and includes the effect of compounding interest.

ww.They are identical in every sense and bo: They are not identical, because APR states the yearly cost of borrowing while APY states yearly earnings after compounding, so the two figures describe different things.
ww.APY applies to credit cards only, and ne: APY is not limited to credit cards, since it is the standard way banks quote what savings accounts and deposits earn once compounding is included.
ww.APR includes compounding on savings, whi: This reverses the terms: APY is the earnings figure that includes compounding on savings, and APR is the borrowing cost quoted on loans and cards.

rw: An overdraft happens when you spend or withdraw more than the checking balance holds, so the account goes negative and the bank usually charges a fee.

ww.Depositing too much money into the accou: Depositing money raises the balance, so it can never cause a shortfall, and an overdraft is the opposite situation of spending more than you hold.
ww.Earning interest on your savings each mo: Earning interest on savings is a gain on your balance each month, not a shortfall, so it has nothing to do with overdrawing a checking account.
ww.Closing an account at a bank for good th: Closing an account ends the relationship with the bank, but an overdraft is a negative balance caused by spending beyond what the account actually holds.

rw: A certificate of deposit locks money for a fixed term such as a year in return for a higher rate than ordinary accounts, which suits money not needed soon.

ww.A prepaid card account: A prepaid card holds only the money loaded onto it and generally pays no interest, so it would not offer the best return for a year of saving.
ww.A cash envelope fund: A cash envelope fund keeps physical money at home or in a drawer, which earns no interest at all, so it cannot pay the highest rate.
ww.A basic checking account: A basic checking account is built for everyday spending and normally pays little or no interest, so it is a poor choice for money left alone for a year.

rw: The National Credit Union Administration insures credit union deposits, usually up to $250,000 per depositor, through its share insurance fund, which is the credit union counterpart of FDIC coverage.

ww.SEC: The SEC regulates securities markets and investor disclosure, and it does not insure deposits at credit unions or banks against the failure of the institution.
ww.FDIC: The FDIC insures deposits at banks and savings associations, but credit unions are covered by a separate federal insurer, the NCUA, rather than by the FDIC.
ww.FINRA: FINRA is a self-regulatory body that oversees brokerage firms and their sales practices, and it provides no deposit insurance for credit union members.

rw: The standard FDIC insurance amount is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category, so a single account is protected up to that sum.

ww.$25,000: $25,000 is far below the real limit, because the standard FDIC coverage amount has been $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category for many years.
ww.$1,000,000: $1,000,000 overstates the coverage, since it is four times the real $250,000 limit, though people can exceed $250,000 in total by using several ownership categories or banks.
ww.$100,000: $100,000 was the old limit before it was raised to $250,000 in 2008 and then made permanent, so it no longer reflects current FDIC coverage.

rw: A routing number is a nine-digit code that identifies the bank or credit union, so checks, direct deposits and transfers get sent to the right institution.

ww.Identifying your PIN number at the ATM s: A PIN is a secret code chosen by the cardholder to authorize ATM use, and it is unrelated to the number printed on checks that identifies the bank.
ww.Showing your balance to the teller at a: A teller can display a balance from your account number and identification, and the routing number does not hold or show any balance information.
ww.Setting your interest rate with the bank: Interest rates are set by the bank's account terms and market conditions, and the routing number is only an identifier and has no influence on the rate.

rw: ACH is an electronic network that moves money from one bank account to another, and it handles direct deposits, bill payments and many online transfers in batches.

ww.A cash withdrawal made at an ATM machine: A cash withdrawal at an ATM takes physical money from your account, and it is not a transfer routed between banks through the Automated Clearing House.
ww.A paper check deposit made at a bank bra: A paper check deposited at a branch is processed as a paper item, and it differs from an ACH transfer, which moves money electronically without any paper.
ww.A credit card swipe at a store counter b: A credit card swipe runs through a card network and creates a loan to be repaid later, whereas ACH moves money directly between bank accounts.

rw: Direct deposit sends wages electronically from the employer straight into the employee's bank account, which is fast and safe and avoids lost or stolen paper checks.

ww.Cash handed to an employee at the end of: Handing cash to an employee is paying in cash, and direct deposit instead sends the pay electronically into the worker's bank account, with no cash changing hands.
ww.A mailed check from the employer to the: A mailed check is a paper payment that must be deposited by the worker, whereas direct deposit sends the money electronically to the account without any mailing.
ww.A loan payment made to the bank by the b: A loan payment goes from the borrower to the bank, and direct deposit runs the other way, with an employer sending wages into the worker's account.

rw: To reconcile is to compare your own records of deposits and spending with the bank statement, so you can find errors, missing items or unauthorized charges.

ww.Change the PIN number on your debit card: Changing a PIN is a security step for a card and has nothing to do with matching your records against the entries on the monthly statement.
ww.Ask for a loan from the bank to pay for: Asking for a loan is a borrowing decision, whereas reconciling is only a check that your own records agree with what the bank has recorded.
ww.Close the account and stop using the ban: Closing the account would end the relationship, but reconciling is a routine check done while the account stays open and in regular use.

rw: The reconciled balance is $820, found by taking the $900 statement figure and subtracting the $80 outstanding check, which matches the $820 in your records.

ww.$980: $980 comes from adding the $80 check to the $900 statement balance, but an outstanding check has not yet cleared, so it must be subtracted, not added.
ww.$900: $900 is only the bank's balance, which has not yet subtracted the outstanding $80 check, so it overstates what you actually have available to spend.
ww.$80: $80 is just the amount of the outstanding check, not a balance, and the reconciled balance is the $900 bank figure minus that $80, giving $820.

rw: Credit card liability for unauthorized use is capped at $50 under federal law, and the disputed money belongs to the lender, so this is the strongest protection.

ww.Debit card: Debit card losses can be larger, because liability depends on how fast you report, and it can reach hundreds of dollars or more, and the money leaves your own account first.
ww.Cash only: Cash only offers no federal fraud protection at all, since stolen or lost cash cannot be recovered or disputed with any bank or card issuer.
ww.Prepaid card: Prepaid cards often lack the federal liability caps that apply to credit cards, so protection depends on the issuer's own terms and may be weaker.

rw: A stop-payment order tells your bank not to honor a specific check you wrote, which is useful if it is lost, stolen or issued by mistake.

ww.A tax form filed with the revenue agency: A tax form is filed with a revenue agency to report income and does not instruct a bank to refuse a particular check from your account.
ww.A request to close a loan that has been: Closing a loan that has been paid off is a different request, and a stop-payment order concerns one check, not the end of a loan.
ww.A way to deposit cash into any account a: Depositing cash at an ATM puts money into an account, whereas a stop-payment order blocks a check from being paid out of your account.

rw: Mobile check deposit means using a banking app to photograph the front and back of a check, and the bank credits the funds without a branch visit.

ww.Mailing cash to the bank in an envelope: Mailing cash is risky and unrelated to mobile deposit, which lets you deposit a check electronically through an app without sending anything physical to the bank.
ww.Cashing at a store only, where the clerk: Cashing a check at a store is a different service done in person with a clerk, and mobile deposit instead puts the check into your account using a phone.
ww.Withdrawing cash at an ATM machine near: Withdrawing cash at an ATM takes money out of your account, while mobile check deposit does the opposite by adding the value of a check.

rw: A minimum balance requirement is the lowest amount an account must hold, often daily or monthly, and falling below it can trigger a monthly maintenance fee.

ww.The highest amount allowed in an account: The highest amount allowed before a fee describes a cap, which accounts rarely have, whereas a minimum balance is a floor that you must stay above.
ww.A loan amount borrowed from a bank by th: A loan amount is money borrowed from a bank, while a minimum balance concerns the money you hold in an account and the fees tied to it.
ww.The interest rate on the account paid by: The interest rate is what the bank pays on deposits, and it is a separate account term from the minimum balance needed to avoid fees.

rw: FICO scores range from 300 to 850, with higher scores signalling lower credit risk, and this scale is the widely used standard for lenders reviewing applications.

ww.500 to 1500: 500 to 1500 does not match any FICO scale, and 1500 is far above the real maximum of 850 used by the FICO scoring model.
ww.100 to 500: 100 to 500 is not the FICO range, since the lowest real score is 300 and the top is 850, so this range is far too low.
ww.0 to 100: 0 to 100 resembles a percentage scale, but FICO scores run from 300 to 850, so a range ending at 100 is far too small.

rw: Payment history carries the largest weight at about 35 percent of a FICO score, because paying on time shows lenders how reliably you repay borrowed money.

ww.Age of your car: The age of your car is not part of a credit report, because FICO looks at financial behavior such as payments and debt, not what vehicle you own.
ww.Credit mix used: Credit mix is only about 10 percent of the score, so it counts for far less than payment history, which carries roughly 35 percent.
ww.New credit use: New credit accounts for about 10 percent of the score, which is much smaller than the 35 percent given to payment history and the 30 percent for amounts owed.

rw: Amounts owed, including how much of your available credit you use, makes up roughly 30 percent of a FICO score, the second largest factor after payment history.

ww.5%: 5% is far too small, because amounts owed is one of the biggest factors and carries about 30 percent of the score, behind only payment history.
ww.0%: 0% is wrong, since utilization and debt levels matter a lot to lenders, and they are weighted at roughly 30 percent of a FICO score.
ww.60%: 60% would be larger than payment history at 35 percent, which is the biggest factor, so amounts owed cannot weigh that much in a FICO score.

rw: Utilization is the balance divided by the credit limit, so $1,500 divided by $5,000 equals 0.30, which is 30 percent of the available credit being used.

ww.15%: 15% would be right for a balance of $750 on a $5,000 limit, but $1,500 divided by $5,000 is 0.30, so the rate is higher than 15%.
ww.70%: 70% is not close, since $1,500 is only a small part of the limit, and $1,500 divided by $5,000 equals 0.30 and not 0.70.
ww.3.3%: 3.3% looks like the ratio flipped, where $5,000 divided by $1,500 is about 3.3, but utilization is balance over limit, which is 1,500 over 5,000.

rw: Keeping utilization below 30 percent is the common guideline, because using a smaller share of your available credit looks responsible and tends to raise scores.

ww.Above 90%: Utilization above 90% means nearly all available credit is used, which signals high risk to lenders and normally lowers a credit score significantly.
ww.Exactly 100%: Exactly 100% means the card is fully maxed out, which is among the worst utilization levels and strongly hurts a credit score.
ww.Over limit: Going over the limit means utilization above 100 percent, which risks fees and declined payments, and it is far worse for a credit score than a low balance.

rw: A soft inquiry is a credit check that does not affect your score, such as looking at your own report or a lender's pre-approval screening.

ww.A missed payment reported to the credit: A missed payment reported to the bureaus is a negative mark that can lower the score, and it is not an inquiry at all.
ww.A loan application sent to a bank for a: A loan application usually triggers a hard inquiry, which can slightly lower your score, so it is the opposite of a soft inquiry.
ww.A collection account opened by a debt co: A collection account is a debt passed to a collector, which appears as a negative item and can damage a score, unlike a harmless soft inquiry.

rw: Most negative items such as late payments, collections and charge-offs can remain for up to seven years, and bankruptcies can stay as long as ten years.

ww.Never removed: Negative items do not stay forever, because the Fair Credit Reporting Act limits most of them to a set time before they must be removed from reports.
ww.One month only: One month is far too short, as late payments and collections generally stay on a credit report for several years, not just a single month.
ww.About two years: Two years is too short for most negative items, since late payments and collections remain for longer, though hard inquiries do fall off after about two years.

rw: The three bureaus currently offer free weekly reports at AnnualCreditReport.com, an expansion of the older once-a-year rule that began during the pandemic and continued permanently.

ww.Only after a bankruptcy filing: Free reports are not limited to people who filed bankruptcy, since every consumer can request them from each of the three bureaus through the official site.
ww.Once every ten years, at most: Once every ten years is far too rare, because the bureaus now offer free reports much more often than that to every consumer.
ww.Never, as banks refuse to give them: The claim that banks refuse to give reports is false, because federal law gives consumers the right to free credit reports from the bureaus.

rw: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion are the three major credit bureaus, the companies that collect your credit history and sell reports and scores to lenders.

ww.IRS, SEC and FDIC, three agencies: The IRS, SEC and FDIC are government agencies for taxes, securities and deposit insurance, and none of them is a credit bureau that tracks your borrowing.
ww.FICO, Visa and Mastercard firms: FICO is a scoring company, while Visa and Mastercard are payment networks, so this group does not name the three bureaus that hold credit reports.
ww.Fidelity, Vanguard and Schwab: Fidelity, Vanguard and Schwab are investment firms that offer brokerage and funds, and they do not collect or report consumer credit history.

rw: A secured credit card is backed by a cash deposit that sets the limit, and on-time payments get reported to the bureaus, which helps build credit.

ww.A debit card linked to your own checking: A debit card draws on your own checking account and is not credit, so it cannot build credit history the way a secured credit card does.
ww.A card for the wealthy only, with no lim: A secured card is not for the wealthy, since it requires a refundable deposit and is usually aimed at people building or repairing their credit.
ww.A card with no limit on what you can spe: A secured card has a limit, which usually equals the deposit you put down, so it does not allow unlimited spending each month.

rw: A secured loan is backed by collateral such as a house or car that the lender can claim if you default, while an unsecured loan has none.

ww.Secured loans have no repayment schedule: Secured loans do have repayment schedules, and what defines them is collateral, so saying they have none is wrong, as is claiming unsecured loans differ in payment timing.
ww.Unsecured loans are always cheaper than: Unsecured loans are not always cheaper, because with no collateral for the lender to claim they typically carry higher interest rates than secured loans.
ww.They are identical in every way and have: They are not identical, because collateral is the key difference, and that changes the risk to the lender and usually the interest rate offered.

rw: A mortgage is secured because the home itself serves as collateral, so the lender can foreclose and sell it if the borrower stops paying.

ww.Revolving credit, which can be reused: Revolving credit, like a credit card, lets you borrow and repay repeatedly up to a limit, whereas a mortgage is a fixed loan that ends when repaid.
ww.Unsecured, with no collateral at all: Unsecured loans have no collateral, but a mortgage always does, since the house is pledged to the lender until the loan is fully repaid.
ww.A payday loan from a short-term lender: A payday loan is a short-term, high-cost loan, and a mortgage is a long-term home loan with a much lower rate and a repayment of many years.

rw: Revolving credit, such as a credit card or line of credit, lets you borrow, repay and borrow again as long as you stay within the limit.

ww.A tax refund paid by the government each: A tax refund is money returned by the government after overpayment, not a form of credit, and it does not involve borrowing and reusing funds up to a limit.
ww.A loan with equal payments that ends whe: A loan with equal payments that ends when repaid describes installment credit, while revolving credit stays open and can be used again after you repay.
ww.A one-time cash gift from a relative or: A one-time gift from a relative is not credit, since credit means borrowed money that must be repaid, and a gift has no repayment attached.

rw: Installment credit is a loan repaid in equal payments over a set period, as with car loans, student loans and mortgages, until the balance reaches zero.

ww.A rewards program run by a store or a ba: A store or bank rewards program gives points or cash back, and it is not a loan, so it is not installment credit.
ww.A savings plan held at a bank for the fu: A savings plan holds your own money for the future, whereas installment credit means you borrow money and pay it back over time.
ww.A credit line you reuse as you repay, up: A credit line you reuse as you repay describes revolving credit like a credit card, while an installment loan is a fixed amount repaid on a schedule.

rw: The grace period is the time after the statement closes during which paying the full balance means no interest is charged on new purchases.

ww.Time before you get the card, while the: Time spent waiting for approval before the card arrives is just the application process, and it is not the interest-free window after a statement closes.
ww.A penalty period that starts after a lat: A penalty period after a late payment is not a grace period, since the grace period is a benefit that avoids interest rather than a punishment.
ww.The loan term agreed with the lender at: The loan term is how long you have to repay a loan, which is a different idea from the short interest-free window the grace period offers on cards.

rw: Paying the minimum leaves interest accumulating on the unpaid balance, so the debt lasts much longer and total interest paid becomes far larger than it first seems.

ww.Interest stops being charged after the f: Interest does not stop after the minimum payment, because any unpaid balance keeps accruing interest each month, so the debt can grow instead of shrinking quickly.
ww.The balance disappears quickly, since in: The balance does not disappear quickly, because minimum payments mostly cover interest, and the remaining balance keeps charging interest, which slows the payoff dramatically.
ww.The credit limit is erased from the card: A bank does not erase the credit limit because of minimum payments, since paying at least the minimum keeps the account in good standing.

rw: A balance transfer moves debt from one card to another, often to take advantage of a lower or zero introductory rate, which can cut interest costs.

ww.Opening a savings account with a small d: Opening a savings account is a deposit that earns interest, whereas a balance transfer is about moving existing debt between credit cards.
ww.Paying a bill with cash at the counter o: Paying a bill with cash at a counter settles a purchase directly and involves no moving of card debt from one lender to another.
ww.Closing a card and paying off the whole: Closing a card and paying off the balance ends the debt entirely, whereas a balance transfer shifts it to a different card and keeps it outstanding.

rw: Debt-to-income ratio is your total monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income, and lenders use it to judge whether you can afford new credit.

ww.Income divided by assets owned by the pe: Income divided by assets is not a standard measure, and the debt-to-income ratio instead compares what you owe each month to what you earn.
ww.Interest divided by principal, the yearl: Interest divided by principal gives a rate of return or loan cost, and it is not the ratio that compares monthly debt payments with gross income.
ww.Savings divided by income earned in the: Savings divided by income is a savings rate, and it measures how much you set aside and not how much of your income goes to debts.

rw: Pat's ratio is $900 divided by $3,000, which equals 0.30, or 30 percent, showing the share of gross monthly income that already goes to debts.

ww.90%: 90% would come from mistakenly using 900 as if it were a percentage, but dividing $900 by $3,000 gives 0.30, which is 30 percent.
ww.33%: 33% would come from dividing 1,000 by 3,000, and Pat pays $900, not $1,000, so $900 over $3,000 gives exactly 30 percent.
ww.3%: 3% would drop a zero, but $900 divided by $3,000 equals 0.30, so Pat's debt payments take 30 percent of income and not 3 percent.

rw: The five Cs are character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions, which lenders use to judge how likely a borrower is to repay a loan.

ww.Cost, color, cut, clarity and carat of a: Cost, color, cut, clarity and carat are the four Cs of diamonds plus a repeat, and they have nothing to do with how a lender judges credit.
ww.Chase, Citi, Capital One, Chime and Cash: Chase, Citi, Capital One, Chime and Cash are names of lenders and brands, not qualities that a lender evaluates in a borrower under the five Cs.
ww.Cash, checks, coins, cards and credit li: Cash, checks, coins, cards and credit lines are forms of money and credit, not the five criteria lenders use to judge a loan applicant.

rw: Predatory lending uses unfair, deceptive or abusive practices, such as hidden fees or extreme rates, that trap borrowers in debt they struggle to escape.

ww.Lending between friends at fair rates an: Lending between friends at fair rates is ordinary and harmless, and predatory lending instead exploits borrowers with unfair terms and hidden costs.
ww.Lending at fair rates to people who can: Lending at fair rates to people who can repay is responsible lending, which is the opposite of the exploitative terms found in predatory lending.
ww.Lending only to wealthy people, who can: Lending only to wealthy borrowers is selective lending, not predatory, because predatory lenders usually target vulnerable people with costly and deceptive loans.

rw: The Fair Credit Reporting Act lets you dispute inaccurate or incomplete information, and the bureau must investigate and correct or delete anything it cannot verify.

ww.Hide your report from lenders and credit: The law does not let you hide a report from lenders, since the bureaus may share it with parties who have a permissible purpose.
ww.Remove all negative items at will, true: You cannot have accurate negative items removed by asking, because the Fair Credit Reporting Act only requires removal of information that is inaccurate or unverifiable.
ww.Set your own score at whatever level you: Your credit score is calculated from report data by a scoring model, so you cannot choose it, and the law gives no such right.

rw: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits discrimination in lending based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age or receipt of public assistance.

ww.A ban on all credit checks made by any l: The Act does not ban credit checks, since lenders routinely review credit reports, and it targets unfair discrimination instead of the use of credit information.
ww.A ban on collateral being required by an: Lenders may require collateral for many loans, and the Act deals with discrimination against applicants and not with whether collateral is permitted.
ww.Charging any interest at all on a loan o: Charging interest is legal and normal, and the Act does not ban it, since its purpose is to stop unfair treatment of credit applicants.

rw: Simple interest equals principal times rate times time, so $2,000 times 0.05 times 3 gives $300, with no compounding on earlier interest.

ww.$3,000: $3,000 is the principal plus the interest, since $2,000 plus $1,000 would be needed for that, whereas the simple interest alone is far smaller at $300.
ww.$100: $100 is the interest for only one year at 5 percent, but the question asks for three years, so it must be multiplied by 3.
ww.$315.25: $315.25 is the compound interest figure, which is what yearly compounding would earn, but simple interest has no compounding and is just principal times rate times time.

rw: Simple interest is principal times rate times time, so $1,500 times 0.04 times 2 equals $120 over the two years.

ww.$60: $60 is the interest for only one year, since $1,500 times 0.04 is $60, but the question covers two years, which doubles it.
ww.$240: $240 would double the correct result, as it would arise from using 8 percent or four years, while $1,500 times 0.04 times 2 gives $120.
ww.$1,620: $1,620 is the total balance of principal plus interest, which is $1,500 plus $120, and not the interest alone that the question asks for.

rw: The Rule of 72 divides 72 by the annual rate, so 72 divided by 6 gives about 12 years for money to double.

ww.72 years: 72 years confuses the rule, since you divide 72 by the rate and not use 72 itself, so 72 divided by 6 gives 12 years.
ww.6 years: 6 years just repeats the interest rate, and the Rule of 72 divides 72 by that rate, so 72 divided by 6 is 12.
ww.18 years: 18 years would be right at a rate of 4 percent since 72 divided by 4 is 18, but at 6 percent the answer is shorter.

rw: Dividing 72 by the 9 percent rate gives 8, so money doubles in about 8 years under the Rule of 72.

ww.12 years: 12 years is the doubling time at 6 percent, since 72 divided by 6 is 12, but at 9 percent the doubling is faster.
ww.9 years: 9 years just repeats the rate itself, but the Rule of 72 divides 72 by 9, which gives 8 years, not 9.
ww.6 years: 6 years would need a 12 percent rate, since 72 divided by 12 is 6, while at 9 percent the result is 8 years.

rw: A three-month emergency fund is 3 times $2,400, which equals $7,200, enough to cover essential expenses for three months if income stops.

ww.$2,400: $2,400 is only one month of expenses, so it covers a one-month cushion, while a three-month fund needs three times that amount.
ww.$14,400: $14,400 equals six months of expenses at $2,400 each, so it is double what a three-month emergency fund requires.
ww.$800: $800 is the monthly amount divided by three, which is backwards, since you multiply $2,400 by 3 months to get $7,200.

rw: Six months of essential expenses at $2,000 per month is 6 times $2,000, which equals $12,000 held in easily accessible savings.

ww.$2,000: $2,000 is just one month of essential expenses, so it falls well short of the six months of coverage that the question asks about.
ww.$333: $333 is not close, and it would come from dividing in the wrong direction, while six months requires multiplying $2,000 by 6.
ww.$6,000: $6,000 equals three months of expenses at $2,000 each, which is only half of a six-month emergency fund.

rw: Cash is already money and can be spent immediately with no conversion or loss in value, which makes it the most liquid asset there is.

ww.Land: Land can take months to sell and the price may be uncertain, so it is a low-liquidity asset and not the quickest to convert into spendable money.
ww.A house: A house usually takes weeks or months to sell and involves fees, so it is far less liquid than cash that can be spent right now.
ww.A boat: A boat must be listed and sold to a buyer, which takes time and may force a lower price, so it is not very liquid.

rw: An employer match is money the employer adds to an employee's retirement account based on what the employee contributes, which is effectively free extra compensation.

ww.A fee charged by an employer to the work: The match is a benefit paid to the worker, not a fee charged by the employer, so it never reduces what the employee takes home.
ww.A tax penalty charged by the government: A tax penalty on early withdrawals is imposed by the government, not the employer, and it is separate from the extra contribution that a match provides.
ww.A loan from an employer that the worker: A loan from an employer must be repaid with interest, whereas a match is an outright contribution that never has to be paid back.

rw: Sam contributes 6 percent of $50,000, which is $3,000, and the employer matches 50 percent of that, so the match equals $1,500.

ww.$3,000: $3,000 is the full 6 percent that Sam contributes, which is $50,000 times 0.06, but the employer only matches half of it.
ww.$6,000: $6,000 would be 12 percent of pay, which is double what Sam contributes, so it greatly overstates the match.
ww.$750: $750 is only a quarter of Sam's contribution, but a 50 percent match on $3,000 gives $1,500, so $750 is too low.

rw: With a traditional IRA, contributions may be tax-deductible now, the money grows tax-deferred, and withdrawals in retirement are taxed as ordinary income.

ww.Taxes paid yearly on the growth, with no: Paying tax on growth each year while withdrawals are tax free describes no standard IRA, and a Roth is taxed up front, not yearly.
ww.Taxed twice, once on the contributions a: An IRA does not tax money twice, since contributions are either deducted or taxed once, and then the account is taxed a single time at withdrawal.
ww.No tax ever applies to the account, at a: IRA accounts are not tax-free, since a traditional IRA taxes withdrawals and a Roth taxes the contributions, so some tax applies at some stage.

rw: An HSA is a health savings account used to pay medical costs, available to people covered by a high-deductible health plan, with tax advantages on contributions.

ww.A hospital insurance policy that covers: A hospital insurance policy is a different product, since an HSA is a savings account you fund yourself and not a plan that pays hospital stays.
ww.A home savings account for buying a hous: A home savings account for buying a house is not what HSA stands for, because the H refers to health and not housing.
ww.A holiday spending account for gifts, tr: A holiday spending account is not an HSA, whose letters stand for health savings account and which is designed for medical expenses.

rw: The yearly fee equals the expense ratio times the amount held, so 0.005 times $20,000 equals $100 taken from the fund each year.

ww.$10: $10 would be the fee on only $2,000, but fees at 0.5 percent of $20,000 are ten times larger than that.
ww.$1,000: $1,000 would require a 5 percent expense ratio, which is ten times the stated 0.5 percent, so it greatly overstates the real yearly fees.
ww.$500: $500 would be a 2.5 percent fee, but 0.5 percent of $20,000 is $100, so $500 is five times too much.

rw: An ETF is an exchange-traded fund that holds a basket of assets such as stocks or bonds and trades during the day just like a stock.

ww.A tax form that investors file to report: A tax form for reporting gains is a different document, whereas an ETF is an investment fund that holds a mix of assets.
ww.A type of loan that a brokerage gives so: A brokerage margin loan lets clients borrow to buy shares, and an ETF is an investment product, not a form of credit.
ww.A bank certificate that locks money away: A bank certificate locking money for a fixed term is a certificate of deposit, which is a different product from an exchange-traded fund.

rw: The gain per share is $55 minus $40, which is $15, and multiplying by 20 shares gives a total capital gain of $300.

ww.$800: $800 is the original cost of the shares, which is $40 times 20, and it does not subtract anything, so it is not the gain.
ww.$15: $15 is the gain on a single share, since $55 minus $40 is $15, but Sam holds 20 shares and so the total gain is larger.
ww.$1,100: $1,100 is the total sale value of the shares, which is $55 times 20, and it includes the original cost, so it is not the gain.

rw: The W-4 is given to your employer to say how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck, based on your filing status and allowances.

ww.Reporting wages to the tax authority eac: Reporting wages to the tax authority is done by the employer through the W-2, and the W-4 is a form the employee fills out.
ww.Filing your return with the revenue agen: Filing your return is done with a form such as the 1040, and the W-4 only instructs the employer about withholding from paychecks.
ww.Applying for credit at a bank with a loa: Applying for credit uses a loan application with a lender, and a W-4 is a tax form and has no role in credit approval.

rw: A W-2 is a form from the employer showing your wages for the year and the taxes withheld, which you use when filing your tax return.

ww.A form for independent contractors who a: Independent contractors receive a 1099 form instead, since they are not employees, so a W-2 is not their form for reporting pay.
ww.A form for withholding choices that the: The form that gives withholding choices to the employer is the W-4, which is filled out at hiring, while the W-2 is issued afterward by the employer.
ww.A tax refund check from the revenue agen: A refund is a payment from the tax agency, and a W-2 is only an information form, not a check of any kind.

rw: The 1099 reports income that is not regular wages, such as pay for independent contractors, interest, dividends and other non-wage income, with no tax usually withheld.

ww.Wages from a regular job with a firm, sh: Wages from a regular job with taxes withheld are reported on a W-2, so this describes the W-2 and not the 1099.
ww.Property taxes paid on land and building: Property taxes are billed by local governments and are not reported on a 1099, which is a form for reporting types of income.
ww.Withholding choices that an employee mak: Withholding choices are made on the W-4 when an employee starts a job, and the 1099 is a form that reports income received.

rw: A $1,000 credit cuts the tax bill by the full $1,000, whereas a $1,000 deduction in the 22 percent bracket saves only $1,000 times 0.22, which is $220.

ww.They are equal in the amount of tax that: They are not equal, because a deduction lowers taxable income and saves only your bracket share, while a credit reduces the tax owed dollar for dollar.
ww.The deduction, because it is the bigger: A deduction is not better just because it sounds larger, since $1,000 times the 22 percent bracket only saves $220 while the credit saves $1,000.
ww.Neither one, as both save exactly the sa: They do not save the same amount, since the credit saves $1,000 and the deduction saves about $220 at a 22 percent rate.

rw: The standard deduction is a fixed amount that taxpayers can subtract from their income instead of itemizing deductions, which lowers the income that gets taxed.

ww.A type of credit given to taxpayers who: It is not a credit for people in need, since a credit reduces tax directly while the standard deduction reduces taxable income and is available to most filers.
ww.A penalty charged on late tax returns by: A penalty for late returns is a separate charge, and the standard deduction is a benefit that lowers taxes and not a punishment.
ww.A tax refund paid to people who file the: A refund is money returned after overpayment, whereas the standard deduction is a subtraction from income and does not depend on filing early.

rw: A regressive tax takes a larger share of income from lower earners than from higher earners, as sales taxes often do since poorer households spend more of their income.

ww.A tax that rises with income as a person: A tax that rises with income as earnings grow is progressive, like the income tax brackets, which is the opposite of a regressive tax.
ww.A flat income tax with one single rate f: A flat income tax applies one rate to everyone, so the share of income paid does not fall as income rises, which makes it proportional.
ww.A tax-free zone for businesses and indiv: A tax-free zone has no tax at all, and so it does not describe a regressive tax, which does take money from lower earners.

rw: The marginal tax rate is the rate applied to your next dollar of income, and it is the rate of the highest bracket that your income reaches.

ww.The lowest rate paid on any income earne: The lowest rate paid on any income describes the bottom bracket, not the marginal rate, which is the rate that applies to the last dollar you earn.
ww.The average rate on all income, tax paid: The average rate is total tax divided by total income, which is the effective rate and differs from the marginal rate on the next dollar.
ww.The sales tax rate on goods you buy in s: A sales tax rate applies to purchases in shops, and it is not the marginal income tax rate on additional earnings.

rw: In a progressive system only the income above the bracket threshold is taxed at the higher rate, and the income below keeps the lower rates, so a raise never lowers take-home pay.

ww.None of it is taxed at the higher rate: Some of the extra income is taxed at the higher rate, so saying none is false, since the portion above the threshold lands in the higher bracket.
ww.Only your savings are taxed at the highe: Savings are not taxed by bracket in this way, because brackets apply to taxable income of all kinds and not just to money saved.
ww.All your income is taxed at the higher r: Only the part above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so your earlier income stays taxed at the lower rates, and it is a myth that all income is hit.

rw: The FICA share is 7.65 percent of $2,000, which is 2,000 times 0.0765, and equals $153 withheld for Social Security and Medicare.

ww.$15.30: $15.30 is only 0.765 percent of $2,000, which is one tenth of the correct figure, so the decimal point has been misplaced by one place.
ww.$765: $765 is ten times too large, because 7.65 percent of $2,000 is $153 and not $765, which would be a 38 percent rate.
ww.$7.65: $7.65 is the rate itself written as dollars, but 7.65 percent of a $2,000 paycheck is $153, so this value is far too small.

rw: Individual federal income tax returns are normally due on April 15, unless that date falls on a weekend or holiday, when the deadline moves to the next business day.

ww.December 31: December 31 is the end of the tax year, and not the filing deadline, since returns for that year are filed in the following spring.
ww.July 4: July 4 is a national holiday, not a tax deadline, and individual returns are normally due on April 15 each year.
ww.January 1: January 1 begins the new tax year and is a holiday, so it is not the filing deadline, which falls in mid April.

rw: If you owe tax and file late without an extension, the agency can charge a failure-to-file penalty plus interest, so you may owe more than the original tax.

ww.You get a bonus from the tax office: Filing late does not earn a bonus, since the tax agency charges penalties and interest on unpaid tax and does not reward late filing.
ww.Nothing happens at all to your return: Something does happen, because the agency assesses penalties and interest on any unpaid tax, so late filing is not free of consequences.
ww.The debt is erased by the tax agency: The tax agency does not erase debt for late filing, and the amount owed remains due along with added penalties and interest.

rw: A property tax is charged on real estate you own, such as land and buildings, usually by local governments, and funds schools and local services.

ww.A tax on food bought at a shop: A tax on food bought at a shop is a sales tax, applied at purchase, rather than a property tax on assets that you own.
ww.A tax on wages and salaries: A tax on wages and salaries is an income or payroll tax, and a property tax is instead charged on assets such as land and buildings.
ww.A tax on gifts and legacies: A tax on gifts and legacies is a gift or inheritance tax, which differs from a property tax on real estate you own.

rw: A sales tax is a percentage added to the price of goods and services at the time of purchase, and the seller collects it for the government.

ww.A tax on property such as land and build: A tax on property such as land and buildings is a property tax, which is charged on ownership and not added at checkout.
ww.A tax on wages and salaries earned by wo: A tax on wages and salaries earned is an income or payroll tax, which is taken from pay and not added to the price of goods.
ww.A tax on inheritances received after a r: A tax on inheritances is an estate or inheritance tax, which applies after someone dies and not at the point of sale.

rw: The earned income tax credit is a refundable credit for low-to-moderate income working people, and it can reduce tax owed or increase a refund.

ww.A student loan program for people in col: A student loan program is a way to borrow for school, but the EITC is a tax credit for working people with limited income.
ww.A tax on high earners paid on top of inc: A tax on high earners is the opposite of the EITC, which gives money back to workers with lower or moderate incomes.
ww.A bank bonus paid for opening a new acco: A bank bonus for opening an account is a private promotion, and the EITC is a government tax credit and has nothing to do with banks.

rw: You pay the $500 deductible first, and the insurer pays the rest, so $2,500 minus $500 means the insurer pays $2,000 of the repair.

ww.$3,000: $3,000 is the repair cost plus the deductible, but the deductible is what you pay yourself, so the insurer pays less than the bill, not more.
ww.$500: $500 is just the deductible, which is the part you pay, and the insurer covers the remaining $2,000 of the $2,500 bill.
ww.$2,500: $2,500 would be the full cost, but a deductible means you pay $500 first, so the insurer cannot cover the whole bill.

rw: A copayment is a fixed fee you pay for a covered service, such as $25 for a doctor visit, with the insurer paying the remainder.

ww.A tax charged on each visit to the docto: A copayment is a set fee paid to the provider for care and not a tax, and nothing about it is a government charge.
ww.The deductible you pay before coverage s: The deductible is the amount you pay before coverage starts, which differs from a copayment, a fixed fee for a specific service.
ww.A yearly fee paid to the insurance compa: A yearly fee paid to the insurance company is the premium, or an annual charge, which is not the per-service copayment.

rw: Coinsurance is the percentage of covered costs you pay after meeting the deductible, such as 20 percent, with the insurer paying the other 80 percent.

ww.A flat fee you pay at every visit to a d: A flat fee at every visit is a copayment, and coinsurance is instead a percentage of the cost that you share with the insurer.
ww.The monthly premium you pay to keep the: The monthly amount paid to keep the policy active is the premium, which is a separate cost from coinsurance on medical bills.
ww.A type of tax charged on medical care an: Coinsurance is a cost-sharing arrangement within the policy and not a tax on medical care, and it is never levied by the government.

rw: Liability insurance pays for injury or property damage that you cause to other people, including legal costs, up to the policy limits.

ww.Your lost income from a missed paycheck: Lost income from a missed paycheck is covered, if at all, by disability or income protection, not by liability insurance, which concerns harm to others.
ww.Your own car repairs after a crash you c: Your own car repairs after a crash you cause fall under collision coverage, while liability covers the other party's damages and not yours.
ww.Your medical bills after any kind of cra: Your own medical bills are covered by health insurance or medical payments coverage, whereas liability pays for injuries suffered by others.

rw: Comprehensive coverage pays for non-collision damage to your car, such as theft, hail, fire, vandalism or hitting an animal, subject to your deductible.

ww.Routine maintenance such as oil changes: Routine maintenance such as oil changes and tires is a normal ownership cost, and auto insurance does not pay for it.
ww.Injuries to others in a crash that you c: Injuries to others in a crash you cause are covered by liability coverage, which is a separate part of the auto policy.
ww.Accident damage to your car from a colli: Accident damage from hitting another vehicle or object is covered by collision coverage, whereas comprehensive deals with other events.

rw: Uninsured motorist coverage helps pay your costs when you are hit by a driver who has no insurance, so you are not left with the bills.

ww.Coverage for rental cars hired on vacati: Rental cars on vacation are handled by separate rental coverage, and uninsured motorist coverage concerns other drivers who lack insurance.
ww.Coverage for glass in the windows and do: Glass damage is usually handled under comprehensive coverage, and it is not what uninsured motorist coverage is designed to pay for.
ww.Coverage for your own accidents, whoever: Your own accidents regardless of fault describe collision coverage, but uninsured motorist coverage only applies when another driver without insurance causes the harm.

rw: Homeowners insurance covers damage to the home, personal belongings and liability for injuries on the property, up to policy limits and subject to exclusions.

ww.A mortgage payment you make to your bank: A mortgage payment repays a home loan to a bank, which differs from homeowners insurance, a policy that protects the house and belongings.
ww.A property tax charged on land and build: A property tax is charged by the local government on land and buildings, and it is not insurance, which protects against loss.
ww.A policy for renters who lease flats fro: A policy for renters is renters insurance, which covers belongings and liability of tenants, while homeowners insurance is meant for those who own the home.

rw: Whole life provides coverage for your entire life as long as premiums are paid, and it builds a cash value that you can borrow against.

ww.Health coverage for illness and injury o: Coverage for health illness and injury only describes health insurance, whereas whole life insurance pays a death benefit and builds cash value.
ww.No payout is ever made to anyone at any: Whole life insurance pays a death benefit to the beneficiary, so saying no payout is ever made is false and defeats its purpose.
ww.Coverage for a set term, ending after so: Coverage for a set term ending after some years is term life insurance, which is different from whole life that lasts for life.

rw: The beneficiary is the person or entity named in the policy to receive the death benefit when the insured person dies.

ww.The insurer that issues the policy to yo: The insurer is the company that issues the policy and pays the claim, whereas the beneficiary is the person who receives the payout.
ww.The doctor who treats the insured person: A doctor treats the insured person and has no claim to the benefit, so the doctor is not the beneficiary.
ww.The agent who sold you the life policy: The agent who sold the policy earns a commission and is not the beneficiary, who is the person named to receive the payout.

rw: The purpose of insurance is to transfer the financial risk of a possible loss to an insurer in exchange for paying a premium.

ww.To prevent all losses from ever happenin: Insurance cannot prevent losses from happening, since it only pays for part or all of the cost afterward, so the claim of preventing all losses is wrong.
ww.To avoid paying taxes on income earned b: Insurance is not a way to avoid taxes, since premiums are a cost and the purpose is to cover losses and not to cut taxes.
ww.To guarantee profits to every policyhold: Insurance does not guarantee profit to policyholders, because it pays only for covered losses, and most people pay premiums without ever filing a claim.

rw: Self-insurance means setting aside money, such as an emergency fund, to pay for potential losses yourself rather than buying a policy from an insurer.

ww.Borrowing from friends when a loss occur: Borrowing from friends after a loss is just taking a loan, whereas self-insurance means setting aside your own money in advance to cover possible losses.
ww.Ignoring risk and hoping that no loss wi: Ignoring risk and hoping no loss occurs is not self-insurance, because there is no plan or funds ready to cover a loss.
ww.Buying a policy from an insurer to cover: Buying a policy from an insurer is ordinary insurance, which transfers risk, while self-insurance means you keep the risk and cover it yourself.

rw: The marketplace is an exchange where individuals and families can compare and buy health plans, and many qualify for subsidies that lower the premium.

ww.A stock exchange for trading shares in p: A stock exchange trades company shares, while the Affordable Care Act marketplace is a place to compare and buy health insurance plans.
ww.A bank that lends money to people who ne: The marketplace is not a bank and makes no loans, and it simply lets people shop for health plans and see any subsidies for which they qualify.
ww.A tax office that processes returns for: A tax office processes returns, but the marketplace is where health plans are chosen, and it is not a government revenue office.

rw: An HMO generally requires you to use in-network providers and to get referrals from a primary care doctor to see specialists, in exchange for lower costs.

ww.A bank that holds the savings of members: An HMO is a type of health plan and not a bank, and it does not hold savings accounts for members.
ww.A plan with no network of doctors and no: A plan with no network and no referrals describes the opposite of an HMO, which depends on a defined network and referral rules.
ww.A pharmacy that sells medicines and heal: An HMO is a health plan, not a pharmacy, so it does not sell medicines to the public, though it may cover prescriptions.

rw: A PPO offers more flexibility, letting you see out-of-network providers without a referral, though you usually pay more than for in-network care.

ww.A plan with no coverage for doctors or h: A plan with no coverage for doctors or hospitals would be pointless, whereas a PPO provides coverage and a network of preferred providers.
ww.A pharmacy that sells medicines and heal: A PPO is a health plan and not a pharmacy, so it does not sell medicines directly to people in town.
ww.A bank that lends money to patients who: A PPO is a health plan and not a bank, and it does not lend money to patients to help pay for their own plans.

rw: Keeping records supports filing taxes, budgeting and proving transactions, so you can track spending, resolve disputes and answer audits with evidence.

ww.They prevent saving money for the future: Records support saving and planning by showing where money goes, so claiming they prevent saving is false and goes against their purpose.
ww.They increase debt over time and cut you: Good records help control debt and savings, and they do not increase debt, since tracking spending lets you spot problems and cut costs.
ww.They are never needed by anyone for any: Records are needed for taxes, disputes, loans and insurance claims, so claiming no one ever needs them for any purpose is plainly false.

rw: The usual guidance is to keep returns and supporting documents at least three years, since that is the normal audit window, and longer in some cases.

ww.Only one month after you file them, no m: One month is too short, because the tax agency can audit returns for years after filing, so you need to keep them far longer.
ww.They never need keeping, the agency has: Keeping a copy is your responsibility, and you cannot rely on the agency having one, since you may need your own records to support deductions.
ww.Only one week after you file them, no mo: One week is far too short, since an audit or amended return can come years later, so the records must be kept much longer.

rw: A will is a legal document that states how your property is to be distributed after your death and who will manage the estate.

ww.A tax return that reports a person's inc: A tax return reports income and taxes to the government, and it is unrelated to the distribution of property after death.
ww.A bank form that lets a customer name wh: A bank form that lets someone use an account describes a joint account or authorized user agreement, which is different from a will.
ww.A loan contract that sets the payments a: A loan contract sets the repayment terms for a borrower, while a will states how your belongings are passed on after you die.

rw: Net worth equals assets minus liabilities, so $60,000 minus $22,000 gives $38,000, which is what Alex would have left after paying every debt.

ww.$82,000: $82,000 adds the debts to the assets, but net worth is assets minus liabilities, so you subtract the $22,000 owed from the $60,000 owned.
ww.$60,000: $60,000 is only the value of Alex's assets, and it ignores the $22,000 of debts that must be subtracted to find net worth.
ww.$22,000: $22,000 is only the amount Alex owes, and net worth requires subtracting that from the $60,000 of assets, giving $38,000.

rw: A savings account balance is money that you own and can use, so it is an asset that adds to your net worth.

ww.A credit card balance owed: A credit card balance owed is money you must pay to the issuer, which makes it a liability and not an asset.
ww.A mortgage balance still owed: A mortgage balance still owed is a debt to the lender, so it is a liability and not something you own.
ww.A student loan balance: A student loan balance is money you owe, so it is a liability that reduces your net worth rather than increasing it.

rw: An auto loan balance is money you owe to a lender, which makes it a liability that subtracts from your net worth.

ww.A savings account: A savings account is money you own, so it is an asset and not a liability, since you do not owe it to anyone.
ww.A house you own outright: A house you own outright is something of value that you hold, so it is an asset, and no debt remains on it.
ww.A retirement account: A retirement account holds savings that belong to you, so it is an asset and not a debt that you owe.

rw: A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, which makes it clear enough to plan for and to track over time.

ww.Secret, mild, active, rare and trivial g: Secret, mild, active, rare and trivial do not describe SMART goals, since secret and trivial goals would be hard to plan or measure.
ww.Sudden, major, awkward, rich and thin go: Sudden, major, awkward, rich and thin are not the SMART terms, and these words would not help anyone set a workable goal.
ww.Simple, minor, average, random and tiny,: Simple, minor, average, random and tiny are not what the letters stand for, which are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

rw: Saving $1,800 for a laptop by December at $150 a month is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, since 12 months times $150 equals $1,800.

ww.Spend less money on random things whenev: Spending less on random things is vague, with no amount or deadline, so it is not specific, measurable or time-bound, and fails the SMART test.
ww.Be rich someday, with no plan and no cle: Being rich someday has no amount, plan or deadline, so it is neither specific nor measurable and does not meet the SMART standard.
ww.Save more someday when you have the time: Saving more someday has no amount and no date, which makes it vague and impossible to measure, so it is not a SMART goal.

rw: A short-term financial goal is one you aim to reach within about a year, such as building a small emergency fund or paying off a card.

ww.A goal that takes thirty years to reach: A goal that takes thirty years to reach is a long-term goal, not a short-term one, which is reached within about a year.
ww.A goal with no set timeline at all, ever: A goal with no timeline is not short-term, because short-term goals have a clear timeframe, and having no end date makes progress hard to track.
ww.A goal for retirement in forty years: A goal for retirement in forty years is a long-term goal, since short-term goals are completed in about a year or less.

rw: A long-term financial goal takes many years to reach, such as retirement, buying a home or paying for a child's college education.

ww.A weekend purchase of a movie ticket or: A weekend movie ticket or meal out is a small near-term expense, so it is a short-term spending item and not a long-term goal.
ww.Saving for lunch or a snack at the end o: Saving for lunch or a snack at the end of the week is a very short-term need and not a goal that takes years.
ww.A monthly bill paid to a utility company: A monthly bill paid to a utility or lender is a recurring expense and not a goal, and it is settled within weeks.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice, such as the other way you could spend money.

ww.The price of a product at the time it is: The price of a product at purchase is its cost, and opportunity cost is the value of what you give up by choosing it.
ww.The interest on a loan or credit card ba: Interest on a loan or card balance is a financing cost, which is a real payment and is different from the value of a forgone alternative.
ww.The sales tax on a purchase made at the: Sales tax is an added charge on a purchase and is a cost you actually pay, while opportunity cost concerns the alternative you give up.

rw: A scam is a deceptive scheme meant to steal money or personal information, often by posing as a trusted business, agency or person.

ww.A legitimate investment offered by a reg: A legitimate investment from a registered firm is lawful and transparent, so it is the opposite of a scam, which aims to deceive.
ww.A bank statement showing deposits and wi: A bank statement is an ordinary record of deposits and withdrawals, and it is a true account of activity and not a deceptive scheme.
ww.A government benefit paid to people who: A government benefit paid to qualifying people is a lawful program and not a trick, so it is not a scam.

rw: Contact the bank using a phone number or app you already know and trust, not the link in the text, which may be a phishing attempt.

ww.Reply with your PIN and the number on th: Replying with your PIN and the number on your card gives a criminal what is needed to steal from you, so never do that.
ww.Click the link at once to unlock your ac: Clicking the link at once is exactly what the scammer wants, because the link probably leads to a fake site that steals your login details.
ww.Forward it to friends and ask them to ch: Forwarding the message to friends spreads the scam and puts them at risk, and they cannot safely judge a suspicious link for you.

rw: Guaranteed high returns with no risk are a classic sign of possible investment fraud, because real investments with higher returns always carry some risk of loss.

ww.A government bond fund: A government bond fund is a real investment with modest returns and some risk, and it does not promise guaranteed high returns without risk.
ww.A bank savings product: A bank savings product pays modest interest and is insured up to limits, and it does not promise high returns without any risk.
ww.A safe, high-return plan: A safe, high-return plan with no risk does not exist in legitimate markets, because higher returns come with higher risk, so the promise is a warning sign.

rw: A long, unique password for each account, stored in a password manager, means one breach cannot unlock your other accounts, so this is the strong practice.

ww.Sharing it with friends so they can log: Sharing a password with friends lets others access your accounts and money, and it is unsafe even if you trust them.
ww.Writing it on your phone case where anyo: Writing a password on your phone case lets anyone who sees it log in, so it offers no protection at all.
ww.Using one simple password everywhere, ch: Using one simple password everywhere means a single breach exposes every account, and changing it only when asked leaves long periods of risk.

rw: Two-factor authentication requires two different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a code sent to your phone, which makes stolen passwords far less useful.

ww.Logging in twice with the same password: Logging in twice with the same password is still one factor, because both entries rely on the same secret that could be stolen.
ww.Using two passwords of different lengths: Two passwords of different lengths are still the same kind of factor, something you know, so this does not meet the two-factor idea.
ww.Using two banks at once to hold your fun: Holding funds at two banks is a way of spreading money around and has nothing to do with proving your identity at login.

rw: The CFPB is a federal agency that protects consumers in financial products and services, taking complaints and enforcing rules on lenders, banks and credit reporting.

ww.A bank that lends money to the general p: The CFPB is a federal agency and not a bank, so it does not lend money to the public, and its role is protection.
ww.A credit bureau that tracks the scores o: Credit bureaus such as Equifax, Experian and TransUnion track credit scores, whereas the CFPB is a regulator that oversees how financial companies treat consumers.
ww.A stock exchange that lists the shares o: A stock exchange lists shares of public companies, and the CFPB is a consumer protection agency that does not run a market.

rw: The APR reflects the yearly cost of carrying a balance on the card, and it shows how much interest you pay if you do not pay in full.

ww.The rewards rate paid on the card: The rewards rate is what you earn back on purchases and is a separate feature, not the interest rate measured by the APR.
ww.The credit limit set for the card: The credit limit is the most you can borrow on the card, and it is not what the annual percentage rate measures.
ww.The annual fee only, charged once a year: The annual fee is a separate flat charge, whereas the APR is about interest, so it is not tied only to the yearly fee.

rw: An annual fee is a yearly charge that some credit cards impose simply for holding the card, whether or not you carry a balance.

ww.A late fee charged when a payment is mad: A late fee is charged when a payment arrives after its due date, which is a different charge from the yearly fee for having a card.
ww.Interest on balances that are carried ov: Interest on balances carried from month to month is the finance charge, and the annual fee is a separate flat yearly cost.
ww.A tax charged by the government on each: An annual fee is set by the card issuer and is not a government tax, so the claim that it is a tax is false.

rw: The avalanche method puts extra money toward the highest-interest debt first while paying minimums elsewhere, which cuts total interest cost and clears debt fastest in dollar terms.

ww.Paying the lowest-interest debt first, c: Paying the lowest-interest debt first leaves the costliest balances growing faster, so you pay more interest overall than if you target the highest rate.
ww.Paying only minimums on all of the debts: Paying only minimums on all debts keeps balances alive for years and lets interest pile up, which is slower and more costly than extra payments.
ww.Ignoring debts and hoping they go away o: Ignoring debts lets interest and fees grow and can lead to collections and credit damage, so debts never go away on their own.

rw: The debt snowball method pays off the smallest debts first while making minimum payments on the others, which builds momentum and motivation as each balance disappears.

ww.Skipping payments for several months in: Skipping payments brings late fees, interest and credit damage, so it does not help clear debt and is not the snowball method.
ww.Taking on more debt each month to cover: Taking on more debt each month to cover old debts only grows the problem, so it is the reverse of the snowball method.
ww.Paying off the largest debt first, whate: Paying off the largest debt first is not the snowball method, which begins with the smallest balance, to build momentum through quick wins.
